# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

DEPARTMENT OF COMMERCE

Census Bureau


Agency Information Collection Activities; Submission to the 
Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for Review and Approval; Comment 
Request; Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)

AGENCY: U.S. Census Bureau, Commerce.

ACTION: Notice of information collection, request for comment.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Department of Commerce, in accordance with the Paperwork 
Reduction Act (PRA) of 1995, invites the general public and other 
Federal agencies to comment on proposed and continuing information 
collections. These comments help us assess the impact of our 
information collection requirements and minimize the public's reporting 
burden. The purpose of this notice is to allow for 60 days of public 
comment on the proposed revision of the Survey of Income and Program 
Participation (SIPP), prior to the submission of the information 
collection request (ICR) to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) 
for approval.

DATES: To ensure consideration, comments regarding this proposed 
information collection must be received on or before October 6, 2026.

ADDRESSES: Interested persons are invited to submit written comments by 
email to [email protected]. Please reference SIPP OMB Comments in 
the subject line of your comments. You may also submit comments, 
identified by Docket Number USBC-2026-0364, to the Federal e-Rulemaking 
Portal: http://www.regulations.gov. All comments received are part of 
the public record. No comments will be posted to http://www.regulations.gov for public viewing until after the comment period 
has closed. Comments will generally be posted without change. All 
Personally Identifiable Information (for example, name and address) 
voluntarily submitted by the commenter may be publicly accessible. Do 
not submit Confidential Business Information or otherwise sensitive or 
protected information. You may submit attachments to electronic 
comments in Microsoft Word, Excel, or Adobe PDF file formats.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Requests for additional information or 
specific questions related to collection activities should be directed 
to Sharon Stern, Assistant Division Chief and SIPP Program Director, 
301-763-5638, [email protected].

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Abstract

    The U.S. Census Bureau plans to request clearance from the Office 
of Management and Budget (OMB) for a field test of the Survey of Income 
and Program Participation (SIPP) in calendar year 2027. This collection 
will be in lieu of a national collection using the questionnaires, 
systems, and processes in place since 2014.
    Since 1983, SIPP has been the primary source of information about 
annual and sub-annual dynamics of income, families and households, 
movement into and out of government programs, and interactions of these 
topics in a single, unified dataset

[[Page 51148]]

allowing for in-depth, informed analyses. Government domestic policy 
formulators and evaluators depend heavily upon the information 
collected in the SIPP in their analyses of the distribution of income 
received either directly as money or indirectly as in-kind benefits and 
the effect of tax and transfer programs on that distribution. They also 
rely on the SIPP data to provide improved and expanded information on 
the dynamics of income and the general economic and financial situation 
of the U.S. population in the context of the household situation. The 
SIPP has measured levels of economic well-being and permitted 
measurement of sub-annual and annual changes in these levels over time.
    Since the inception of the program, SIPP has been an interviewer-
administered household-based survey. Each panel featured a nationally 
representative sample of addresses whose household members were 
interviewed either in person or over the phone several times over a 
multi-year period. In recent years, SIPP has been researching new 
methods to mitigate concerns related to increasing costs for 
interviewer-administered surveys, declining response rates among 
sampled addresses, and increasing attrition of responding households in 
subsequent panels.
    At the forefront of SIPP modernization efforts is the adoption of a 
self-administered internet survey as the primary mode for data 
collection with targeted in-person interviewing of a select number of 
non-responding households. The addition of a SIPP self-response mode is 
one element of a larger, bureau-wide effort to modernize data 
collection systems.
    As SIPP is the premier source of comprehensive information on the 
dynamics of income, employment, household composition, and government 
program participation, testing the impact of the multi-mode data 
collection, statistical methods improvements, and agency-wide 
collection and processing systems is critical. The Census Bureau is 
implementing a multi-year testing strategy. In the summer of 2026, the 
Census Bureau is conducting an internet self-response field test using 
a subset of the redesigned SIPP instrument items on a national sample 
to assess the feasibility of a self-administered data collection (OMB 
number 0607-0978).
    The goals of the 2027 SIPP field test are to build upon the 2026 
test by adding content to the questionnaire; introducing a multi-mode 
survey that incorporates both self-response and non-response computer 
assisted personal interviewing (CAPI); introducing alternative sample 
and weighting methodologies; and using the Census Bureau's Business 
Ecosystem entities for all aspects of the survey process. We will use 
the test to evaluate the frame, sample, weighting, and non-response 
bias; to demonstrate the application of the new systems and processes 
to the SIPP design; research additional opportunities to reduce 
respondent burden through the use of administrative data systems; and 
to assess the quality of key estimates using the new methodologies. The 
2027 SIPP field test will be an important step toward building the 
modern program.
    The design of the test survey is purposefully scalable, as the 
future SIPP design is expected to be. The sample size listed in this 
notice is based on initial budget estimates and allows for expansion. 
The multi-mode data collection vision for the SIPP program includes a 
dual-sample design. One part of the sample will be invited to respond 
through a web-mode instrument only. The second sample component will be 
invited to self-respond on the internet. Among that group, non-
respondents will be contacted for in-person interviews.

II. Method of Collection

    The 2027 SIPP will use a web instrument for both the internet Self-
Response (ISR) and the CAPI modes of data collection. All sampled 
households will receivemail invitations to complete the survey online. 
To increase sample representativeness, field representatives will be 
sent to a small number of nonresponding ISR cases to administer the 
survey in person. The redesigned SIPP interview consists of one adult 
answering questions about each member of the household and uses a six-
month reference period. In instances where the residence is not 
accessible or the respondent makes a request, the field representative 
may conduct the interview by telephone.

III. Data

    OMB Control Number: 0607-1000.
    Form Number(s): SIPP ISR Web Instrument (no form number), SIPP 
nonresponse follow-up CAPI electronic instrument (no form number).
    Type of Review: Regular submission, New Information Collection 
Request.
    Affected Public: Individuals or households.
    Estimated Number of Respondents: 6,000.
    Estimated Time per Response: 40 minutes to respond to survey and 10 
total minutes for reading contact materials.
    Estimated Number of Non-Respondents: 14,000.
    Estimated Time per Non-response: 10 minutes.
    Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours: We estimate 5,000 burden hours 
from those responding to the survey and 2,334 burden hours from 
households that do not respond to the survey for a total of 7,334 
hours.
    Estimated Total Annual Cost to Public: $0 (This is not the cost of 
respondents' time, but the indirect costs respondents may incur for 
such things as purchases of specialized software or hardware needed to 
report, or expenditures for accounting or records maintenance services 
required specifically by the collection.)
    Respondent's Obligation: Voluntary.
    Legal Authority: Title 13, United States Code, Sections 141 and 
182.

IV. Request for Comments

    We are soliciting public comments to permit the Department/Bureau 
to: (a) Evaluate whether the proposed information collection is 
necessary for the proper functions of the Department, including whether 
the information will have practical utility; (b) Evaluate the accuracy 
of our estimate of the time and cost burden for this proposed 
collection, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions 
used; (c) Evaluate ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of 
the information to be collected; and (d) Minimize the reporting burden 
on those who are to respond, including the use of automated collection 
techniques or other forms of information technology.
    Comments that you submit in response to this notice are a matter of 
public record. We will include, or summarize, each comment in our 
request to OMB to approve this ICR. Before including your address, 
phone number, email address, or other personal identifying information 
in your comment, you should be aware that your entire comment--
including your personal identifying information--may be made publicly 
available at any time. While you may ask us in your comment to withhold 
your personal identifying information from public review, we cannot 
guarantee that we will be able to do so.

Sheleen Dumas,
Departmental PRA Compliance Officer, Office of the Under Secretary for 
Economic Affairs, Commerce Department.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)
Description: The Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) is a nationally representative longitudinal survey that provides comprehensive information on the dynamics of income, employment, household composition, and government program participation. SIPP is also a leading source of data on economic well-being, family dynamics, education, wealth, health insurance, child care, and food security. The survey interviews individuals for several years and provides monthly data about changes in household and family composition and economic circumstances over time.
URL: https://census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP)
## Research and preservation report

**Research checked:** October 9, 2026  
**Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce  
**Official website:** https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html

## Executive findings

Your dataset title, description, and URL are substantially correct. SIPP is a nationally representative longitudinal survey designed to explain **how people’s economic circumstances change**, rather than merely describe them at one point in time.

Four qualifications are important:

1. **SIPP is a continuing survey program and a family of datasets—not one file.** Its products include public-use microdata, replicate weights, longitudinal weights, historical topical modules, tables, documentation, and restricted or synthetic linked-data products.
2. **Monthly information does not mean monthly interviews.** For the redesigned survey underlying recent releases, respondents were generally interviewed annually about the preceding calendar year, using an Event History Calendar to reconstruct monthly circumstances.
3. **The year in a release’s name is not its reference year.** The latest release identified, **2025 SIPP**, was published July 15, 2026, and covers January–December **2024**.
4. **The program is entering another consequential redesign.** An August 2026 Federal Register notice proposes a 2027 field test **instead of a national collection using the systems and questionnaire in place since 2014**. Historical descriptions should therefore not be treated as guarantees about future collection.

**Overall assessment:** SIPP has very high research and preservation value. Its distinguishing contribution is the integration of income, employment, household relationships, assets, insurance, and program participation within the same longitudinal records. Its main vulnerabilities are declining response, attrition, complex weighting, changes in collection design, and the loss of interpretability if data are separated from their documentation.

Sources: [SIPP homepage](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html), [2025 release announcement](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/2025-sipp.html), [2026 Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-07/html/2026-16188.htm).

---

## 1. Dataset identity and verified description

### Recommended catalog description

> The Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP) is a U.S. Census Bureau longitudinal household survey representing the U.S. civilian, noninstitutionalized population. It collects detailed information on income, employment, government program participation, household and family composition, and related dimensions of economic well-being. Depending on the panel and release, topics include education, assets and debts, health insurance, disability, child care, child support, and food security. Respondents are followed over multiple years, allowing analysis of monthly circumstances, transitions, and spells. Interview schedules, reference periods, questionnaire content, file organization, and longitudinal coverage vary across survey designs.

This preserves your description’s substance while avoiding the implication that every variable is monthly or every panel has the same duration.

### Core metadata

| Element | Finding |
|---|---|
| Official title | Survey of Income and Program Participation |
| Acronym | SIPP |
| Creator and publisher | U.S. Census Bureau |
| Parent department | U.S. Department of Commerce |
| Resource type | Longitudinal sample survey; multiple statistical data products |
| Geographic scope | United States; primarily national analysis, with selected state-level products |
| Target population | Civilian, noninstitutionalized population |
| Main units represented | Persons, person-months, households, families, and spells, depending on analysis |
| Operational beginning | October 1983; first panel conventionally called the 1984 Panel |
| Recent interview design | Annual retrospective interviews, generally spanning four waves |
| Latest release located | 2025 SIPP, released July 15, 2026 |
| Latest release reference period | January–December 2024 |
| Public-use formats | SAS, Stata, and pipe-delimited text, compressed as ZIP archives |
| General data contact | census.sipp@census.gov |

A crucial distinction is between the **population represented** and **people answering questions**. Adult or age-eligible respondents provide information about household members, including children; the files are not limited to the people personally interviewed.

Sources: [2025 Users’ Guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf), [2025 datasets](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets/2025-data/2025.html).

---

## 2. Who produces and maintains it?

The Census Bureau is responsible for sampling, collection, processing, statistical estimation, disclosure protection, documentation, and publication.

The 2025 Users’ Guide identifies contributions from:

- **Social, Economic, and Housing Statistics Division (SEHSD):** subject-matter expertise and SIPP coordination and outreach.
- **Demographic Statistical Methods Division (DSMD):** sampling, weighting, variance estimation, and methodological documentation.
- **Associate Director for Demographic Programs, Survey Operations:** survey operations and the SIPP survey team.

The survey also supports interagency research. For example, certain linked-data products involve the Social Security Administration and Internal Revenue Service. Those collaborations do **not** make SSA or IRS the publisher of the ordinary SIPP public-use files.

For library authority records, **U.S. Census Bureau** is the appropriate principal corporate creator. Add collaborating agencies when cataloging a particular linked or jointly produced resource.

Source: [2025 Users’ Guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf).

---

## 3. Legal authority, purpose, and confidentiality

### Collection authority

Federal Register notices identify:

- **Title 13, U.S. Code, Section 141**
- **Title 13, U.S. Code, Section 182**

as legal authority for SIPP.

Section 182 authorizes surveys supplying statistical information on population characteristics between censuses. The Bureau’s respondent FAQ specifically cites Section 182; formal collection notices cite both sections.

### Authority is not a requirement to answer

**Participation is voluntary.** SIPP should not be confused with the decennial census or the American Community Survey’s mandatory response requirements.

Also distinguish legal authority from a dataset-specific statutory mandate. The sources reviewed establish that Census is authorized to conduct SIPP and explain its policy purpose; they do not establish an unconditional requirement to conduct an unchanged SIPP every year.

### Paperwork Reduction Act oversight

The main collection is associated with **OMB control number 0607-1000**. Changes undergo Paperwork Reduction Act review, with opportunities for public comment on necessity, utility, burden, and methodology.

A separate **2026 internet self-response field test** operates under **0607-0978**. This explains why some online participation materials show a different number. A preservation record should retain the relevant control number for the particular instrument and collection—not assign one number indiscriminately to every SIPP activity.

### Confidentiality

**Title 13, Section 9** protects identifiable responses and limits their use to statistical purposes. Census states that employees and others with access are subject to serious penalties for unlawful disclosure.

The public-use files are not raw identifiable responses. They undergo disclosure protection, including:

- Topcoding and bottomcoding.
- Perturbation of selected characteristics and event dates.
- Geographic suppression.
- Suppression of variables with insufficient case counts.
- Aggregation of some detailed classifications.

These protections affect analytical interpretation, particularly in distributional tails and detailed demographic analysis.

Sources: [Respondent FAQ](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/information/sipp-faqs.html), [2022 collection notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2022-08-22/html/2022-18059.htm), [2026 notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-07/html/2026-16188.htm), [2025 Users’ Guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf).

---

## 4. History and major changes

| Period | Development and significance |
|---|---|
| **1975–1980** | The Department of Health, Education, and Welfare initiated development of a longitudinal income survey through the Income Survey Development Program, working with Census. Tests included approximately 2,000 households in 1978 and a national sample of 8,200 in 1979. |
| **1981** | Development stopped after funding was lost. |
| **October 1983** | Census received funding and launched operational interviewing. The first panel is called the **1984 Panel**, explaining apparent disagreement between “1983” and “1984” start dates. |
| **Original design** | More than 20,000 households; interviews every four months about the preceding four months; approximately 32 months of follow-up for the initial panel. |
| **Pre-2014 panels** | Panels varied in size, duration, and overlap. Repeated core questions were supplemented by topical modules. The 2008 Panel ultimately had 16 waves, with collection extending into 2013. |
| **2006 onward** | Imminent cancellation prompted a major redesign. Census’s history says stakeholder support helped save the survey, but cost and burden reduction remained priorities. |
| **2014 redesign** | A rebuilt instrument introduced annual interviewing, a one-year reference period, and an Event History Calendar. First interviews began in February 2014. |
| **2018 onward** | SIPP moved to staggered, overlapping panels, introducing new samples annually. Annual release names refer to the collection year across participating panels. |
| **2019 exception** | The 2019 Panel was discontinued after its first wave. Collection problems led Census to prioritize preserving the 2018 Panel’s longitudinal capacity. |
| **Pandemic period** | Collection and questionnaire adaptations included pandemic-related employment responses and stimulus-payment questions. These are important comparability considerations. |
| **2025 Panel** | A new sampling redesign began; recent releases continue to acknowledge rising collection costs and low response. |
| **2026–2027 modernization** | Internet self-response testing in 2026 and a proposed multimode field test in 2027 introduce another potential methodological discontinuity. |

**Preservation implication:** SIPP is not one uniform time series. Preserve panel-specific methods and distinguish genuine social changes from changes in instruments, sampling, processing, and disclosure protection.

Sources: [Census historical account](https://www.census.gov/about/history/historical-censuses-and-surveys/census-programs-surveys/demographic/survey-of-income-and-program-participation.html), [SIPP introduction and history](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/about/sipp-introduction-history.html), [2025 Users’ Guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf).

---

## 5. Current status: a redesign that deserves monitoring

The August 7, 2026 Federal Register notice is especially important for preservationists and policy users.

It proposes:

- A **2027 field test in lieu of national collection using the post-2014 systems and questionnaire**.
- Internet self-response as the primary collection mode.
- Targeted in-person follow-up of selected nonresponding households.
- A web instrument for both self-response and interviewer administration.
- **One adult answering for all household members**.
- A **six-month reference period**, rather than the recent one-year period.
- Testing alternative sample and weighting methods.
- Additional research into administrative-data use to reduce burden.
- An estimated **6,000 responding households**, with scalability depending on resources.

These are **proposed testing arrangements**, not evidence that a comparable replacement national dataset has already been produced. Nor does the notice alone establish that SIPP has permanently ended.

### Questions worth tracking

- Will there be a gap in nationally comparable annual data?
- What happens to existing longitudinal cohorts?
- Which topics and monthly detail survive the redesign?
- How will web-only participation affect coverage and nonresponse bias?
- Will Census publish bridge studies comparing old and new designs?
- Will test data, instrument versions, evaluation reports, and final decisions be publicly available?

The notice’s comment deadline was October 6, 2026. Its docket is **USBC-2026-0364**. Comments themselves are public records; sensitive personal information should not be submitted.

Source: [Full Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-07/html/2026-16188.htm).

---

## 6. What SIPP measures

Content varies across panels and years. Major subject areas include:

| Area | Examples |
|---|---|
| Income | Earnings, retirement income, Social Security, unemployment insurance, other cash income |
| Employment | Employment and unemployment spells, jobs, earnings, reasons for not working |
| Public programs | SNAP, TANF, SSI, WIC, housing assistance, Medicaid, Medicare, school meals |
| Household and family dynamics | Living arrangements, relationships, moves, household membership changes |
| Wealth and debt | Home equity, retirement accounts, vehicles, credit cards, student loans, other assets and liabilities |
| Health and insurance | Coverage types and spells, disability, selected health and medical-expenditure information |
| Education | Attainment, enrollment, credentials and certifications |
| Children and caregiving | Child care, child support, family circumstances |
| Material well-being | Food security and related economic hardship measures |
| Demographics | Age, sex, race, ethnicity, nativity, citizenship, and other characteristics |

### The distinguishing feature: linked circumstances over time

SIPP can help answer:

- How long does poverty last?
- Does job loss precede loss of health insurance?
- How quickly do households enter assistance programs after income falls?
- How do divorce, childbirth, or household moves interact with economic resources?
- Which people appear eligible for a program but do not participate?
- How do wealth and debt differ across demographic groups?

However, **not every topic is observed monthly**. An annual or point-in-time asset measure may be repeated on multiple person-month rows. Repeated values do not turn it into a monthly measurement.

Sources: [Uses of SIPP](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/about/Uses-of-SIPP.html), [2025 Users’ Guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf).

---

## 7. Survey design, coverage, and recent scale

### Sampling and follow-up

SIPP uses a **complex probability sample**, not a simple random sample. Its design involves geographic sampling units and household selection.

Original sample members are generally followed when they move, including when they form new households. People living with them may enter the observed household roster. Follow-up rules have exceptions, including some children moving without an adult original sample member.

The recent design generally provides up to four annual interviews, although actual panel histories differ.

### 2025 collection

Census reports approximately:

- **38,000 designated housing units sampled**.
- **32,500 eligible housing units**.
- **14,000 interviewed households**.
- **32,000 person interviews**, conducted February–June 2025.

The public-use file contains **32,052 persons** and **379,215 person-month records**.

The release combines:

- 2022 Panel, Wave 4.
- 2023 Panel, Wave 3.
- 2024 Panel, Wave 2.
- 2025 Panel, Wave 1.

All contribute information about **2024**. Therefore, “2025 SIPP” and “2025 Panel” are not interchangeable.

### Coverage limitations

SIPP is not a survey of the institutionalized population or a general census of everyone living in the United States. Address-based household sampling also creates challenges for people without stable housing.

Public geography is restricted. Addresses, individual metropolitan areas, and detailed county identifiers are not generally available in public-use files. Selected state-level products exist, but that does not make every state estimate—or small subgroup within a state—reliable.

Sources: [2025 Users’ Guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf), [2025 Source and Accuracy Statement](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/source-accuracy-statements/2025/SIPP-2025-SA.pdf).

---

## 8. Typical users and documented applications

Census identifies several concrete users:

| User | Documented application |
|---|---|
| **U.S. Department of Agriculture** | SNAP participation and eligibility-policy analysis |
| **Social Security Administration** | Long-term benefit projections and retirement-income analysis |
| **Congressional Budget Office** | Program-cost projections, eligible nonparticipants, demographic change |
| **Congressional Research Service** | Policy research on unemployment, insurance gaps, TANF, and Medicaid |
| **Department of Labor** | Characteristics of workers with and without pension or health-plan coverage |
| **Consumer Financial Protection Bureau** | Medical billing and collections among older Americans |
| **Federal Reserve Banks** | Wealth, earnings, mobility, asset use, and demographic disparities |
| **Pew Research Center** | Household wealth differences by race, ethnicity, and other characteristics |

Other typical users include academic economists, sociologists, demographers, public-health researchers, policy institutes, journalists, graduate students, and advocacy organizations.

### Benefits to the public

SIPP supports:

- **Safety-net accountability:** examining whom programs reach and who may be left out.
- **Better policy design:** understanding interactions between work, family circumstances, income, and benefits.
- **Economic-security measurement:** distinguishing temporary hardship from persistent disadvantage.
- **Equity analysis:** examining disparities in wealth, income, insurance, and assistance.
- **Retirement and disability planning:** supplying household context absent from many administrative records.
- **Public transparency:** allowing independent researchers to test claims using public-use data.

These are information benefits, not proof that any particular policy improved outcomes. Causal claims require an appropriate research design.

Sources: [2026 factsheet](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/about/information/2026/2026_SIPP_Factsheet.pdf), [earlier factsheet](https://www.census.gov/content/dam/Census/programs-surveys/sipp/about/SIPP_Factsheet.pdf).

---

## 9. Access routes and related products

### A. Public-use downloadable microdata

Start at the [dataset catalog](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets.html).

Recent releases provide:

- Primary response microdata.
- Replicate-weight files.
- Two-, three-, and four-year longitudinal-weight files.
- Documentation and release notes.

Recent formats are SAS, Stata, and pipe-delimited text in ZIP archives. Historical formats and file structures differ.

For substantial longitudinal analysis or preservation, bulk downloads are preferable to relying exclusively on an interactive service.

### B. Census Microdata API and tabulation tools

SIPP is available through the [Census Microdata API](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/census-microdata-api.SIPP.html), including a 2025 endpoint. Current documentation states that API queries require a key.

Census also documents the **Microdata Access Tool (MDAT)** for custom tabulations and extracts.

Do not assume a web tool supports every longitudinal operation or reproduces every published estimate. Check variable availability, universes, weights, and uncertainty calculations. Archive returned data and query specifications, not just an API URL.

### C. Published tables and reports

Census publishes program-participation tables, wealth and debt tables, poverty briefs, working papers, and other summaries.

Examples include:

- *Wealth of Households: 2024*, using 2025 SIPP.
- Monthly and episodic poverty estimates.
- Tables on Social Security, SNAP, TANF, SSI, WIC, retirement income, unemployment insurance, and child support.

These products are useful for accessible statistics and for checking independently produced estimates.

### D. Restricted-use data

Researchers with approved **Federal Statistical Research Data Center** projects can access more detailed confidential SIPP data.

Access is controlled; project approval, security requirements, and disclosure review apply. Public-use redistribution rights do not extend to confidential files.

### E. SIPP Synthetic Beta

The **SIPP Synthetic Beta (SSB)** is a distinct linked-data resource integrating selected SIPP variables with SSA/IRS earnings and SSA benefit records.

Version 7.0 is based on nine historical panels: 1984, 1990, 1991, 1992, 1993, 1996, 2001, 2004, and 2008.

Important qualifications:

- Values are synthesized/modelled, not simply anonymized originals.
- Access requires an application.
- Census provides a process for validating results against confidential data.
- Census strongly discourages publication of unvalidated synthetic-data findings and does not guarantee their validity.

Preserve SSB as a separate resource with its own version, codebook, access rules, and validation provenance.

Source: [Synthetic SIPP documentation](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/guidance/sipp-synthetic-beta-data-product.html).

---

## 10. Data structure and analytical requirements

### Person-month organization

The recent primary file contains up to 12 records per person:

- Household variables may be repeated across household members.
- Person characteristics may be repeated across months.
- Spell variables may be repeated throughout a spell.
- Genuine monthly variables may change each month.

**Consequences:** summing repeated annual income or household wealth across all rows can multiply amounts incorrectly. Household estimates require a documented household-level selection strategy.

### Identification and joining

Retain all documented identifiers needed to distinguish sample origin, persons, households, and reference months. Verify merge keys against the release-specific documentation.

Do not assume that:

- A person identifier alone is globally unique.
- Every person appears in every release.
- Household membership remains constant.
- A current household identifier represents an unchanging family over time.

### Weight selection

The 2025 Source and Accuracy Statement identifies:

| Analysis | Weight guidance |
|---|---|
| Monthly cross-section | `WPFINWGT` |
| Calendar-year cross-section | `WPFINWGT` when `MONTHCODE=12`, following the guide’s annual-estimation rules |
| Multiyear longitudinal analysis | `FINYR2`, `FINYR3`, or `FINYR4`, as appropriate |

For example, the 2025 two-year longitudinal weights cover **2023–2024**, not 2024–2025.

Longitudinal weights address defined cohorts and attrition. They are not interchangeable with cross-sectional weights.

### Variance estimation

The 2025 release has **240 replicate weights**. Use the release-specific replication instructions and scaling factors.

Treating SIPP as a simple random sample—or treating repeated person-months as independent observations—can seriously misstate standard errors.

### Missingness, editing, and imputation

A missing value may mean:

- Not in the variable’s universe.
- Suppressed for confidentiality.
- Unavailable or otherwise missing.

Census also imputes some person and item nonresponse. Allocation/status flags are therefore analytically important. Published variables may be edited or recoded, and may not correspond one-to-one with questionnaire responses.

Sources: [2025 Users’ Guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf), [Source and Accuracy Statement](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/source-accuracy-statements/2025/SIPP-2025-SA.pdf), [2018+ data primer](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/SIPP_Data_Primer_MAY24.pdf).

---

## 11. Quality issues and interpretive limitations

### Declining response and attrition

The 2025 cross-sectional weighted response rate was **42.63%**.

For the 2025 release’s longitudinal cohorts, Census reports:

| Cohort | Weighted longitudinal response rate |
|---|---:|
| Two-year | 61.67% |
| Three-year | 42.42% |
| Four-year | 25.75% |

These longitudinal rates use different denominators from the cross-sectional rate; they should not be compared as though measuring the same thing.

Weights adjust for nonresponse, but cannot guarantee elimination of bias if nonrespondents differ in ways the adjustments do not capture. Attrition also reduces precision and complicates long-spell analysis.

### Other limitations

- **Recall error:** retrospective monthly histories depend on respondents’ memory.
- **Boundary effects:** reported transitions may cluster around reference-period boundaries.
- **Proxy reporting:** one person may not know another household member’s earnings, insurance, or benefits accurately.
- **Program underreporting:** survey participation counts may differ from administrative totals.
- **Definition differences:** survey households, families, and program eligibility units are not identical.
- **Disclosure protection:** topcoding and perturbation affect extremes and precise event timing.
- **Small samples:** detailed subgroup and state estimates may be unstable.
- **Comparability breaks:** unchanged variable names do not guarantee unchanged measurement.
- **Observational design:** association and temporal ordering are not sufficient to establish causation.
- **Release lag:** monthly detail is not real-time monitoring.

Census explicitly flags [2025 data-quality concerns](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/user-notes/2025-usernotes/2025-data-quality-concerns.html).

### User notes must be treated as part of the dataset

A concrete example: on September 25, 2026, Census reported that the Medicare Part B premium variable **`ESSPARTBKNOW`** was incorrectly capped at **$515** in the 2025 public-use file; the intended cap was **$594**. The note provides case-level corrections.

This matters for analyses of Medicare premiums and Social Security deductions—and demonstrates why a frozen data file without subsequent user notes is an incomplete preservation package.

Source: [2025 Medicare topcoding correction](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/user-notes/2025-usernotes/2025-inc-top-cod-mcr-ded.html).

---

## 12. Relationship to other datasets

This comparison is a practical guide, not a claim that one survey universally replaces another.

| Resource | Prefer it when… | SIPP’s complementary contribution |
|---|---|---|
| **ACS** | You need large-sample geographic profiles and local-area estimates | Longitudinal economic and household transitions |
| **CPS/ASEC** | You need established national labor-force, annual income, or poverty series | Richer monthly histories and integrated program information |
| **Administrative program records** | You need recorded payments or participation in a particular program | Nonparticipants, household context, and cross-program circumstances |
| **Survey of Consumer Finances** | Your priority is detailed wealth measurement, especially the upper tail | Wealth connected to employment, benefits, and family dynamics |
| **PSID** | You need very long-term family and intergenerational follow-up | A different national panel design with extensive program and subannual detail |

SIPP is not generally the best source for county-level advocacy statistics or extreme upper-tail wealth estimates. Its special strength is **economic dynamics within linked household and person histories**.

---

## 13. Reuse, citation, and ethical responsibilities

### Public-use reuse

Ordinary Census-produced public-use data are generally reusable U.S. federal government works, rather than proprietary datasets. Nevertheless:

- Distinguish public-use from restricted-use material.
- Check conditions attached to synthetic-data access and third-party products.
- Do not imply Census endorses independent findings.
- Cite the exact release and file used.

No dataset-specific Creative Commons license or DOI was established in this review; do not invent one in a catalog record.

### Suggested citation

> U.S. Census Bureau. *Survey of Income and Program Participation, 2025: Public-Use Primary Data File*. Reference period January–December 2024. Released July 15, 2026. [File/version identifier], accessed [date]. https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets/2025-data/2025.html.

Also cite weights, relevant technical documents, and any applied corrections. Census’s [citation policy](https://www.census.gov/about/policies/citation.html) recommends identifying title, file/table, vintage, URL, and access date.

### Ethical analysis

Avoid attempting to identify respondents or joining public microdata to identifiable records for reidentification.

For public communication:

- Report uncertainty and unweighted sample sizes.
- Avoid stigmatizing language about benefit recipients.
- Distinguish modelled eligibility from an actual administrative eligibility decision.
- Explain exclusions and representativeness limits.
- Do not infer fraud from survey/administrative discrepancies.

## 14. Preservation priorities and recommended package

**Recommendation: preserve SIPP as a documented collection with versioned dependencies, not as a single spreadsheet.**

### Priority 1: Data and weights

For each release or historical panel, retain:

- Original Census download archives.
- Primary/core files.
- Historical topical modules.
- Replicate-weight files.
- Longitudinal-weight files.
- Any companion status or linkage documentation required for interpretation.

### Priority 2: Representation information

Retain:

- Data dictionaries and value labels.
- Users’ Guides.
- Questionnaires and instrument specifications.
- Source and Accuracy Statements.
- Weight-selection guidance.
- Variable crosswalks between releases.
- Universe definitions.
- Editing, imputation, and disclosure-protection documentation.

### Priority 3: Corrections and provenance

Retain:

- Release notes.
- All applicable user notes and errata.
- Correction tables or patches.
- Original and corrected versions separately.
- Retrieval dates, source URLs, file sizes, and checksums.
- Transformation code and software environment information.

### Priority 4: Program context

Archive:

- Release announcements and publication catalogs.
- Federal Register and OMB materials.
- Historical descriptions.
- Redesign proposals and evaluation reports.
- Published tables and briefs useful for validation.

### Recommended preservation practices

- Generate **SHA-256 checksums** on acquisition.
- Keep original bytes immutable.
- Create open-format derivatives when useful, but preserve labels, missing-value semantics, identifiers, and types.
- Treat Parquet or CSV as derivatives—not replacements for original SAS/Stata files and their metadata.
- Snapshot web documentation; dynamic codebooks and interfaces may not archive completely.
- Maintain a release manifest tying every file to its compatible documentation and weights.
- Assign a repository persistent identifier to the preserved package where appropriate.
- Label public, synthetic, and restricted resources distinctly.
- Run validation checks: row counts, identifier uniqueness, weight merges, and reproduction of selected published estimates.

### Minimum catalog fields

Record:

- Program title.
- Panel and wave, where applicable.
- Collection year.
- Reference period.
- Release date.
- File type and analytical unit.
- Target population and geographic restrictions.
- Original filename and source URL.
- Version/retrieval date and checksum.
- Weight dependencies.
- Related documentation and corrections.
- Access and reuse conditions.

**Preservation risk assessment:** the files are downloadable and documented, but reproducibility is fragile if weights, universes, crosswalks, and errata are lost. The current redesign makes preservation of the existing design especially urgent.

## 15. Recommended actions by audience

### Preservationist
Acquire complete historical and recent release packages, including corrections. Capture the 2026–2027 redesign record while it is current.

### Data librarian
Catalog the program and individual releases separately. Make collection year versus reference year prominent. Identify weight and documentation dependencies.

### Data scientist
Read the release-specific guide before reshaping or pooling files. Validate joins, universes, weighting, and replicate-weight variance estimation. Avoid random train/test splits that leak the same people or households across sets.

### Policy activist
Use published tables where they answer the question adequately. For custom estimates, disclose reference periods, uncertainty, sample sizes, and limitations. Monitor redesign decisions for losses in content, coverage, and longitudinal continuity.

## Scope and remaining uncertainties

This report draws primarily on Census and official Federal Register materials. It verifies the program’s identity, authority, history, recent release, principal access routes, and major analytical concerns.

It is **not** a byte-level audit of every historical file or an exhaustive bibliography of SIPP research. I did not independently download and validate the microdata or establish:

- A complete release-by-release revision ledger.
- Final approval or implementation outcomes for the proposed 2027 design.
- Whether every historical product remains available through every access route.
- A comprehensive historical budget series.
- A dataset-specific DOI or license declaration.

Those are appropriate next steps for a formal archival acquisition.

## Bottom line

SIPP is a major public statistical resource for understanding **economic insecurity, program participation, and household change over time**. Its value lies as much in its relationships, timing, and documentation as in its individual variables. The correct preservation target is therefore the **complete data-and-documentation ecosystem**, including weights, corrections, methodological history, and redesign records.

# SIPP dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**  
**Primary publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau  
**Primary location:** https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp.html

## Overall finding

**The strongest documented risks concern SIPP’s future continuity and comparability—not the disappearance of its historical files.** Historical data remain listed on Census’s servers, and the latest annual release is available. However, Census is testing a substantially different collection design and proposes replacing the established national collection with a field test in 2027. Agency-wide staffing losses add operational risk.

I apply your rubric to **documented conditions as of the assessment date**, distinguishing implemented changes from proposals. Consequently, “No Known Issue” for current publication does **not** mean that future publication is secure.

This is a documentary and availability review, not a complete download-and-checksum audit of every historical file. Advocacy sources are identified as such; proposed budgets are not treated as enacted appropriations.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

**Evidence supporting this level**

- Census’s [dataset catalog](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets.html) continues to offer releases by year for **2018–2025** and by panel/wave for **1984–2014**.
- I checked the live [Census download directory](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets/), which lists historical panel directories and recent annual releases.
- Representative historical directories remain accessible:
  - [1984](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets/1984/) lists full-panel data archives, dictionaries, SAS input programs, and wave directories.
  - [2024](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets/2024/) lists primary microdata, replicate weights, longitudinal weights, schemas, and input examples.

**Evidence relevant to higher levels**

- **Moderate Risk:** Public-use files contain suppressed variables and disclosure protections. These are documented publication procedures, not evidence that previously available historical elements have recently been withdrawn. See the [2025 Users’ Guide](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/methodology/2025_SIPP_Users_Guide.pdf).
- **High Risk / Gone:** I found no documented removal of historical SIPP releases sufficient to support either level.

**Why this level is most appropriate:** Historical files remain publicly listed, with no identified retrospective withdrawal. This finding does not establish byte-for-byte integrity or completeness of every file.

**Preservation implication:** Preserve data together with dictionaries, weights, and user notes. A retained microdata file without its interpretation materials is not a reliably usable copy.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Selected level: **No Known Issue — under the rubric’s current-status tests, with a major forward-looking warning**

**Evidence supporting this level**

- The latest identified annual release, **2025 SIPP**, was published **July 15, 2026**, covering calendar year **2024**. That is consistent with the recent practice of publishing annual files in the year after collection. See the [release announcement](https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2026/2025-sipp.html).
- The main collection’s OMB record, **0607-1000**, identifies approval through **December 31, 2026**. I found no evidence of an expired ICR:
  - [OMB/OIRA record](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAViewICR?ref_nbr=202310-0607-005)
  - [Readable record mirror](https://omb.report/icr/202310-0607-005)
- Census also publishes [2026 participant materials](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/information/sipp-survparticp-materials.html), including returning-participant letters and interviewer materials. Their presence is not proof of completed collection, but cautions against assuming that all regular collection stopped in 2026.

**Evidence relevant to higher levels**

- **High Risk, prospectively:** The [August 7, 2026 Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-07/html/2026-16188.htm) proposes a 2027 field test:
  > “in lieu of a national collection using the questionnaires, systems, and processes in place since 2014.”

  If implemented without a comparable replacement, this would support **High Risk** because a normal national collection would be skipped.
- **Moderate Risk:** Census’s [July 2026 modernization webinar transcript](https://www2.census.gov/about/training-workshops/2026/2026-07-14-sipp-modernization-2026-field-test-update-transcript.pdf) describes a proposed testing timeline extending to a full field test in **2028**, conditional on budget and OMB approval. It establishes continuity uncertainty, but not an already missed publication date.
- **Gone:** No source reviewed establishes permanent termination of all SIPP collection and publication.

**Why this level is most appropriate:** The latest publication and existing clearance satisfy the rubric’s present-tense conditions. The proposed 2027 replacement is serious, but should not be described as an already skipped collection.

**Monitoring trigger:** Reclassify to **High Risk** if Census confirms that the regular national cycle is omitted without a comparable statistical release.

---

## 3. Data Quality

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence supporting this level**

- Census explicitly reports [2025 data-quality concerns](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/user-notes/2025-usernotes/2025-data-quality-concerns.html): declining response rates increase standard errors and weights.
- The [2025 release page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/data/datasets/2025-data/2025.html) identifies rising collection costs and a lower-than-average national unit response rate.
- The proposed 2027 design changes multiple measurement conditions:
  - Internet self-response as the primary mode.
  - Targeted in-person follow-up.
  - One adult reporting for the whole household.
  - A six-month reference period.
  - Alternative sampling and weighting methods.
  - Greater investigation of administrative-data use.

  These create emerging risks to coverage, comparability, longitudinal continuity, and detailed subgroup estimates. Source: [Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-07/html/2026-16188.htm).

**Evidence relevant to other levels**

- **High Risk:** Replacing the regular collection with a smaller field test could reduce effective coverage and continuity. However, the proposal does not establish the final national product’s granularity, release frequency, or timeliness.
- **No Known Issue:** Census says modernization is intended to improve quality and reduce burden. Shorter recall and administrative records could help, but those benefits remain to be demonstrated.
- **Gone:** Collection and publication have not been shown to have permanently ended.

**Why this level is most appropriate:** Emerging risks are documented; an implemented reduction in the published national product’s granularity or frequency is not yet established.

**Accuracy caveat:** Public corrections matter independently of redesign. For example, Census issued a [September 2026 Medicare-premium topcoding correction](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/tech-documentation/user-notes/2025-usernotes/2025-inc-top-cod-mcr-ded.html). Archives should retain the original release and applicable corrections.

## 4. Statutory Context

### Selected level: **High Risk**

**Evidence supporting this level**

- SIPP relies on broad Census authority under **13 U.S.C. §§ 141 and 182**, rather than a SIPP-specific requirement fixing its content, frequency, or publication deadline. The [Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-07/html/2026-16188.htm) identifies these authorities and voluntary participation.
- These provisions authorize statistical collection but leave substantial discretion over how this particular survey operates.
- Other resources—CPS, ACS, and administrative records—provide partial substitutes for income, insurance, demographic, or program-participation statistics. They do **not** fully replace SIPP’s integrated monthly longitudinal information.

**Evidence supporting lower levels**

- **Moderate Risk:** SIPP has important programmatic uses. Census documents use by USDA, SSA, CBO, and CRS for program analysis, projections, and eligibility research. See [Uses of SIPP](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/about/Uses-of-SIPP.html).
- **No Known Issue:** Its named statutory authorities and extensive federal use provide institutional support. However, I did not identify a legal requirement to maintain this particular collection unchanged, or a requirement making SIPP indispensable to program implementation.

**Why this level is most appropriate:** Under your rubric, broad authorization and potential substitutes support **High Risk**. This is a finding about weak protection against discontinuation or substitution—not lack of lawful authority or public value.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

### Selected level: **High Risk**

**Evidence supporting this level**

The strongest quantitative evidence is **Census-wide**, not SIPP-team-specific.

- The American Statistical Association’s [2026 midyear report](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/FedStatHealth_MidYearUpdate.pdf?v=1) reports Census staffing declines across its tracking period:
  - OPM figures: **13,232 → 10,683**, a decline of **2,549**, approximately **19.3%**.
  - Budget-document figures: **8,282 → 7,183**, a decline of **1,099**, approximately **13.3%**.

  These series measure staffing differently and should not be combined. Nevertheless, both exceed your **1,000-person** High Risk threshold.
- The report also identifies continuing leadership instability: the director position remained vacant, with someone performing its duties, as of July 2026.

**Evidence supporting Moderate Risk or providing counterweight**

- Percentage staffing losses fall within your **10–39% Moderate Risk** band. The absolute-loss threshold makes the selected level High Risk.
- ASA reports that enacted FY2026 Census funding increased overall, while the **Current Surveys** account declined about **3% nominally**. That does not meet your budget-cut thresholds.
- Proposed cuts are more severe:
  - FY2026’s request proposed roughly **$40 million** in Current Surveys reductions, principally targeting SIPP.
  - FY2027’s request proposed a substantial reduction in Current Demographic Statistics.

  Sources: [Census Project FY2026 budget analysis](https://thecensusproject.org/2025/06/30/department-of-commerce-releases-fiscal-year-2026-census-budget-details/) and [September 2026 CRS budget overview](https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2026-09-08_IF13308_18f200063d183ce6d1b7a5184be21fc403b54e69.pdf). These proposals should **not** be treated as enacted SIPP-specific cuts.

**Requested staffing tracker**

I reviewed the [USAJobs Listings Tracker](https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com). It states that collection stopped December 31, 2025, and warns that **job listings are not actual hires**. It therefore cannot establish current Census headcount losses or SIPP staffing percentages.

**Gone:** No evidence shows elimination of all Census or SIPP staff or funding.

**Why this level is most appropriate:** Reported agency-wide losses exceed the rubric’s absolute threshold. Confidence is lower regarding how much of that loss directly affects SIPP.

## 6. Policy

### Selected level: **High Risk**

**Evidence supporting this level**

- Since January 2025, the Administration’s budget agenda has specifically targeted SIPP for a smaller, more targeted sample and greater use of nonsurvey data. The [Census Project’s analysis](https://thecensusproject.org/2025/06/30/department-of-commerce-releases-fiscal-year-2026-census-budget-details/) quotes the budget justification’s criticism of the existing survey as expensive and challenging for respondents.
- Modernization is not solely hypothetical: the [Federal Register notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-08-07/html/2026-16188.htm) states that Census was conducting an internet self-response field test in summer 2026.
- The same notice proposes replacing the established national collection in 2027. Together, the budget agenda and implemented testing constitute significant policy-linked change.

**Evidence supporting Moderate Risk**

- The 2027 replacement remains a proposal requiring approval; its final scope and publication consequences are unresolved.
- Modernization also addresses longstanding costs, attrition, and response problems. It should not be assumed that every methodological change was politically initiated.

**Political commentary and user concerns**

- The [Center on Budget and Policy Priorities](https://www.cbpp.org/research/poverty-and-inequality/federal-data-are-disappearing-as-statistical-agencies-face-budget) warns that a reduced SIPP may fail to preserve monthly income and household histories needed to assess benefit eligibility and policy changes.
- The [Census Project](https://thecensusproject.org/2026/08/10/census-bureau-plans-new-sipp-method-field-test/) calls for restored resources and greater transparency about collection and dissemination.

These are stakeholder assessments, not proof of future losses. I found no SIPP-specific presidential order, verified political alteration of historical observations, or permanent termination.

**Why this level is most appropriate:** Significant changes aligned with the Administration’s budget priorities have begun, although important downstream decisions remain pending. This rating does not imply fabricated statistics or deliberate historical-data erasure.
